title: Universal Depot Operator for Stacked EPR Programs
one_liner: One neutral drop-off depot per town that serves batteries, paint, oil containers, textiles and small e-waste for many producer responsibility programs at once.
customer: PROs and stewardship programs (Circular Action Alliance, battery, paint and other stewardship organizations) under a master service agreement, plus host sites paid a host fee.
problem: EPR programs multiply, each building its own thin collection network. Colorado's Interchange 360 (petroleum containers) diverted about 2,500 lb in six months across 10 collection facilities, roughly 250 lb per site. Unit costs per pound are absurd, host sites drown in per-program rules, and households face a different trip per program.
solution: A shared depot at transfer stations and hardware stores with one trained staff, fire-safe cabinets and one weekly consolidated pickup. It is operated under a multi-PRO contract paid per pound plus a site fee. It starts in Colorado and Oregon and adds streams as new programs launch (California's SB 501 medium-format batteries, textiles).
why_now: Colorado's programs are just moving from planning to practice. Oregon's EPR survived the Commerce Clause challenge (Aug 2026) even as NAW appeals, and CAA collected $145.5M in 2025 while spending $56.5M, so budget exists to solve collection cost.
revenue_model: Per-lb handling fees and per-site fees from multiple PROs, host-fee share, and minor resale of recovered commodities.
non_obvious_insight: EPR is designed by material stream but households experience it by trip. The missing layer is a neutral aggregator that turns N programs into one drop-off and one truck.
first_30_days: Meet PRO operations leads in Colorado and Oregon. Pick 3 host sites in one county (a transfer station and 2 hardware stores). Price cabinets and a pickup route. Sign one PRO pilot on cost-plus terms.

title: Fish Settlement Audit Becoming the Fleet's Payment Rail
one_liner: Start by auditing settlement sheets against fish tickets to recover missed money, then become the split-pay rail that routes each settlement to crew, lessors, lenders and the IRS.
customer: Skippers and permit holders who pay $99 flat or 15% of any recovered amount for the audit. Crew use the shares calculator free. Later, skippers and quota lessors pay about 0.3-0.5% of settlement flow for split-pay, and lenders and CFEC-adjacent programs pay referral fees.
problem: The 'price' you're paid is a stack: base price, quality bonuses (for example $0.15 RSW, $0.05 bleeding, $0.05 chilling), loyalty or volume bonuses, post-season retros, and deductions for ice, fuel, gear advances and storage. Every processor's sheet looks different. The fisherman's own copy of the fish ticket sits in a Ziploc in the wheelhouse and never gets matched against the settlement. Nobody checks. Then the whole lump lands in one skipper's account weeks later and he has to act as the bank for crew shares, quota lease payments, loan payments, gear vendors and self-employment tax. That is where disputes, missed quarterly taxes and stiffed crew come from.
solution: Audit: photograph the settlement sheet and fish tickets, and an LLM parses pounds, price stack, bonuses and deductions, flags weight mismatches, missed quality bonuses, wrong grades and unexplained deductions, and prints a plain-English 'you were owed' letter. A crew shares calculator generates crew settlement sheets from the skipper's expense rules. Rail: once trust exists, route the settlement into a virtual account that auto-splits per signed crew share agreement, quota lease, loan payments, vendor invoices and a tax set-aside, with instant partial payments.
why_now: Final settlements for the 2026 salmon season are landing right now (Oct-Dec). Price swung from $1.03 to $1.72 in one year, so fishermen are checking. Vision LLMs can read messy sheets at near-zero cost. Banking-as-a-service and real-time payment rails make split-pay possible for a small team. Crew who waited about four years for crab disaster relief also learned that clean earnings paperwork is worth money.
revenue_model: Audit: $99 flat or 15% of recovery. Rail: 0.3-0.5% of settlement flow plus interchange and float. Later: earned-wage advances against booked settlements, lender referrals, claim-packet prep for federal disaster relief (crew earnings vaults double as the proof), and an anonymized price tape sold to buyers and lenders.
non_obvious_insight: The skipper is the fleet's unlicensed bank, and nobody has both documents in one place. The audit is the trojan horse: it gets a fisherman to hand over settlement history, which is exactly the underwriting and routing data needed for the rail. The settlement sheet is a stack of price components, and the money is hidden in the parts nobody reads.
first_30_days: Post in fishermen's Facebook groups: 'free settlement check, send the sheet.' Process 100 sheets by hand plus LLM, log every error found, and turn 5-10 recoveries into case studies. Build the crew share calculator as a free viral wedge. Charge 15% of recovered amounts above $500. Start collecting the anonymized price stack by port, species and processor.

title: Yes-in-God's-Backyard Deal Desk for Congregations
one_liner: A fixed-fee service that tells a shrinking congregation and its denomination what its land can legally become (by-right housing, ground lease, sale, merger), then runs the governance, title and buyer process.
customer: Regional denominational bodies (presbyteries, dioceses, Methodist conferences, Lutheran synods, synagogue federations) and boards of congregations with 50-250 members that hold a large building and lot they cannot afford to maintain. Secondary payers are affordable-housing developers and community land trusts that need sites.
problem: Per the briefing, only 33% of Americans attend monthly, Christian share has plateaued near 62%, and 18-24-year-olds are only 46% Christian, so many congregations sit on oversized buildings whose upkeep drains endowments. Selling is legally tangled: denominational trust clauses and canon-law approval thresholds, donor-restricted funds and cemeteries, state attorney-general notice for charitable assets, historic designation, and zoning. Lay boards typically wait for a crisis and then accept the first offer, usually an investor or another church. Meanwhile housing-shortage politics have produced by-right housing on religious land laws (California SB 4 took effect in 2024, with similar bills in other states, verify list), so the land may be worth multiples of the building, but few boards know it.
solution: Lead with a $1,500-3,000 'Land Options Report' covering parcel and zoning analysis under the state's faith-land housing law, likely unit yield, estimated residual land value against as-is sale, a title and restriction checklist, and a governance map of who must approve (trust clause, canon law, AG notice). Then sell a fixed-fee 'Transition Package': sequenced legal steps, member-vote scripts and communications, an RFP to pre-qualified faith-friendly developers (ground lease with a worship-space carve-out, so the congregation keeps a chapel and gets rent), and closing management. The report is automated with county parcel data plus LLM extraction of zoning code, reviewed by a real-estate/nonprofit attorney.
why_now: Pew's 2025 finding that decline has leveled but the generational gap is steep (briefing) means closures will keep coming for years. By-right faith-land housing laws are new (California SB 4 effective 2024, more states 2025-26, verify) and few boards know they exist. Cheap parcel data and LLM zoning-code reading make a $1,500 report profitable, where it used to need a $15k consultant.
revenue_model: Report fee of $1.5-3k, paid by congregations or as a bulk judicatory contract of $25-60k per year. Transition package at a fixed $15-40k or 1.5-3% of transaction value. Developer-side site-sourcing retainer or finder's fee, structured around broker-licensing rules.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is not money or developers but a governance process a lay board can survive: each closure has 4-6 approval gates and any one can veto it. The value sits in a pre-mapped approval path for each denomination's polity. Under by-right housing, the residual land value often exceeds the building's as-is price, so the congregation that thinks it must close can instead become a landlord with a rent-paying chapel. Church brokers and developers each see only half of this.
first_30_days: Choose one state with a faith-land housing law and one denomination whose polity is well documented. Offer free Land Options Reports to 10 congregations referred by a regional official, in exchange for case-study rights and a $500 deposit. Hire a part-time real-estate/nonprofit attorney, assemble county GIS and zoning data, and pre-qualify 3 developers. Aim for 3-5 paid reports and one transition engagement within six months.

title: Royalty-Exact Generators: One Adapter per Creator
one_liner: A generative sound-effects and sample tool where every contributor has their own adapter, so payouts are exact by construction instead of guessed after the fact.
customer: Indie game developers, video editors and YouTubers buying sound effects and samples (paying users), with foley artists and sample-pack producers as the opt-in supply side.
problem: Attribution in generative AI is post-hoc guesswork: the Spotify-UMG covers deal promises credit and compensation but discloses no tracking method. Small creators are excluded from label-scale licensing deals. Buyers want output they can use commercially without a legal cloud.
solution: Fine-tune a small open text-to-audio model with a separate adapter per consenting creator. Each generation composes adapters with explicit weights, and royalties follow those weights, so attribution is bookkeeping rather than research. Every output carries a watermark and a per-generation receipt. Start with short sound effects and foley, where inference is cheap, demand is high and buyers' licensing needs are simple.
why_now: Adapter fine-tuning is cheap, Suno's Sep 9 switch to licensed training shows licensed models are becoming the norm, and the credit-and-compensation gap in the Spotify-UMG deal is visible.
revenue_model: $15-50/month subscriptions plus usage credits, with 60-70% distributed to adapter owners pro rata, and enterprise indemnified licenses for studios.
non_obvious_insight: Attribution research tries to recover influence from a monolithic model. Changing the architecture turns attribution into accounting, and small, narrow, licensed models beat large generic ones on legal risk.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 foley artists and sample makers via forums and Gumroad and itch.io sellers. Fine-tune adapters on an open SFX model, demo composite generations with receipts, and pre-sell $99 annual plans to 100 indie developers via itch.io and Discord.

title: Royalty-Paying Archive of Master Tradespeople's Hands
one_liner: Pay retiring master electricians, pipefitters and welders to record expert egocentric video with think-aloud narration, license it to robotics companies, and share royalties with the workers.
customer: Robotics and embodied-AI companies building construction, maintenance and data center installation robots, and foundation-model labs. A second buyer is apprenticeship programs and trade schools, which can license the annotated footage as curriculum.
problem: Egocentric data for robots is being commoditized at the bottom: in September 2026 reporting, gig workers earn about $3-10 an hour filming dishwashing and folding laundry. Expert tasks, like reading a bad splice or feeling a torque, are rare in the data, and the people who know them are retiring, which is also the labor shortage the AI buildout depends on.
solution: Recruit 60+ year-old tradespeople through union retiree halls. Pay $60-120 an hour to wear head and wrist cameras (plus IMU gloves) on real jobs with owner consent, and to narrate why they choose each action and how they detect problems. Add edge-case tagging by a second expert. Blur faces and PII. License datasets by the hour, and pay each worker a royalty of 10-20% of license revenue and a residual on repeat licensing.
why_now: In 2026 papers such as EgoHumanoid showed that robot-free human egocentric demonstrations can train humanoid manipulation directly, so human video is now a working input. The commodity layer is crowded and cheap, so expert-conditioned data is the next premium. Labor and IP disputes over gig data are also starting, which makes a royalty model a moat.
revenue_model: License $150-600 per hour of expert-annotated footage (a hypothesis to test in pilots), exclusivity premiums, and pre-paid data collection contracts. Secondary revenue from trade-school curriculum licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Robotics' bottleneck is shifting from quantity to tacit expertise, and tacit expertise is a wasting asset because its holders are retiring. A royalty share turns those workers from data laborers into stakeholders, which is a legal, ethical and recruiting advantage the $3-an-hour vendors cannot copy.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 retired electricians and pipefitters via IBEW and UA retiree halls and local Facebook groups. Get two robotics startups to pre-pay $25-50k each for 100 hours. Equip people with a $400 kit and a one-page site consent and PII-blur workflow. Deliver the first 20 hours with narration and get a written reference from each buyer.

title: Lake Ice Posts for Ice-Fishing Resorts
one_liner: Cheap solar LoRa thermistor-chain posts frozen into lake ice along access routes, giving resort operators and snowmobile clubs a live thickness trend and rate-of-change alerts on a seasonal subscription.
customer: Ice-fishing resorts and outfitters that rent ice houses and plow ice roads (Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, New York, Maine, Ontario), snowmobile clubs that groom lake trails, ice-derby and tournament organizers, lake associations and rescue units.
problem: Ice thickness varies across a lake and changes fast with warm rain, currents and springs. Resorts rely on daily manual auger checks at a few points. Vehicle and ice-house losses, and deaths, happen. Recent low-ice winters make timing harder. Research-grade buoys exist but cost far too much for a resort, and crowdsourced apps can't watch one specific corridor.
solution: A roughly USD 150 solar post with a thermistor chain spanning air, ice and water, plus a tilt sensor. It infers ice thickness from the 0 degree C interface and gradient, calibrated against the operator's own auger readings. Deploy 3-6 posts along the access road and ice-house village. The dashboard uses plain thresholds by vehicle class, texts an alert on rapid thinning, and offers an embeddable public 'ice conditions' widget for the resort's website.
why_now: It is late September, so units built now can be frozen in for this winter's first ice. LoRa, solar and thermistor chains are commodity. Ice-data apps (satellite radar, crowd reports) prove operators will pay for information, and research-grade buoys have validated the concept, leaving a low-cost tier open.
revenue_model: USD 199 hardware, plus USD 99-249 per post per season. Resort bundle of USD 1,500-4,000 per season. Sponsorship of the public widget by bait shops and outdoor brands. Contract work for counties and rescue units.
non_obvious_insight: Don't sell 'is the ice safe,' which is uncertifiable and a liability trap. Sell operational due diligence and a rate-of-change early warning: ice fails by trend (thermal decay, current), and a fixed post sees the trend before a weekly auger check does. Resorts lose money and reputation when they close roads early or lose a vehicle, so revenue protection is the wedge.
first_30_days: Build 25 posts before first freeze from off-the-shelf thermistor strings, LoRa boards and small solar panels. Sign 4-5 resorts to shoulder-season pilots at cost. Use their daily auger logs as ground truth. Launch a free public ice map to collect crowd calibration points and sponsors. Convert to season subscriptions and use winter data for next year's preorder round.

title: Pull-the-Plug Testing for Hospitals and Water Plants
one_liner: Bring data center-grade full-facility blackout testing to hospitals, water utilities and other critical facilities that never actually pull the plug, and help them source scarce backup gear the AI build-out has hoarded.
customer: Critical-access and rural hospitals, water and wastewater districts, 911 centers, cold-chain warehouses and municipal facilities. Secondary payers: property insurers, hospital captives and risk pools that can subsidize tests or discount premiums for certified resilience.
problem: Routine emergency-power testing is usually a short, partial-load generator run. It rarely exercises the whole chain (utility loss, ATS transfer, sequenced load pickup, cooling, fuel supply, paralleling controls) under real load, so the interaction failures show up during the actual storm or grid event. At the same time the AI build-out has swallowed generator, switchgear and transformer production, with multi-year lead times, so a failed generator or breaker at a small hospital cannot be replaced quickly. Facility managers know their fragile points but have no credible way to test them or to find spares.
solution: A one-day 'controlled blackout' service using data center IST discipline: written sequence-of-operations script, load-bank top-up to real facility load, thermographic and breaker health checks before and after, a witnessed utility-loss transfer, fuel/cooling/ventilation checks, and a punch list. Deliver a resilience certificate with prioritized fixes and remaining-life estimates. Upsell: source and retest certified pre-owned generators, ATS and switchgear from cancelled or paused data center orders, and keep a small regional spares pool for members of a hospital or water-district cooperative.
why_now: AI infrastructure is consuming electrical gear supply (transformer lead times of 3-5 years, switchgear reportedly sold out into 2028) while nearly half of planned 2026 US data center builds are delayed or canceled, which leaves stranded but scarce gear. Storm and grid-stress events are also raising the stakes for small critical facilities. Insurers are scrutinizing resilience, and rural facilities cannot afford the big-firm engineering studies.
revenue_model: $18K-45K per facility test; annual re-test contracts; 10-15% sourcing margin on certified pre-owned gear; insurer or captive partnership fees per policyholder tested; small monthly membership for spares-pool access.
non_obvious_insight: In a data center nobody trusts backup power until someone has pulled the plug at full load, and most first tests find something. The rest of critical infrastructure, which arguably matters more, almost never does this because the fear of a failed test outweighs the fear of a failed emergency. A Cx lead who has run hundreds of pull-the-plug tests can make the test routine and safe. The AI boom also turns the spare-gear problem into a secondary market that only someone who has seen the cancellations firsthand can source from.
first_30_days: Rent a 500 kW-1 MW load bank and partner with an electrical contractor. Call 10 facility directors at critical-access hospitals and rural water districts through state hospital and rural water associations. Offer 2 discounted first tests in exchange for case studies and insurer introductions. Approach one regional property insurer or hospital captive with a loss-prevention pilot. Start a private list of sellers of surplus gensets and switchgear from paused data center projects.

title: Dog Walk Plus: Wellness Checks for Isolated Seniors
one_liner: Turn the daily dog walk at an older client's home into a consented, structured wellness check with escalation, sold to their adult children.
customer: Adult children of independent-living parents who own dogs and live alone (the payer). Later: geriatric care managers, home health agencies, senior housing operators, and long-term care insurers.
problem: A dog walker is the only outsider who enters an older person's home every day at a predictable hour. I have found clients on the floor, and noticed early cognitive decline: the dog fed twice or not at all, pills left out, mail piling up, new bruises. Adult children call and ask us informally, we have no protocol, no consent, and no escalation ladder. Seniors refuse pendants and sensors but accept a walker, because it is about the dog and their dignity stays intact. The dog is also why many seniors delay going to the ER.
solution: A 'Walk Plus' plan built on a written consent from the senior. Alongside the walk, the walker does a 60-second structured check (a 10-tap list covering mobility, orientation, medications visible, food in the fridge, home temperature, bruises, mood, dog condition). Family gets a weekly text summary with trend flags. There is a clear escalation ladder (no answer at the door, then family call, then agreed non-emergency welfare check), and a pet emergency plan with keys and authority on file so that if the owner is hospitalized the walker becomes the dog's custodian. That prevents surrenders and removes the reason to refuse the hospital.
why_now: A large cohort is turning 65 and aging in place, home-care aide capacity is tight, and adult children are stretched thin as remote caregivers. Structured notes are now easy to summarize into a plain-language weekly update. Health plans and senior-service providers are looking for cheap ways to catch problems early, and a daily reason to enter the home is exactly what monitoring products lack.
revenue_model: Walks at $25 to $45 per visit plus a $29 to $49 monthly check-in fee paid by the family. B2B later: license the protocol and reporting to home health agencies and senior housing operators, and sell trend data (with consent) to long-term care insurers or aging-in-place programs.
non_obvious_insight: The dog is the Trojan horse that makes monitoring acceptable. A pendant says 'you're frail'; a dog walker says 'I'm here for the dog.' Walkers already do this informally and unpaid, so the product is less a new service than a protocol, a consent form, and an escalation path around something that already happens every day.
first_30_days: Convert existing senior clients (most walkers have three to six) with a one-page consent form. Build the check-in with a form and Twilio text summaries, no app needed. Partner with two local geriatric care managers who charge by the hour for the same visibility, and post in senior center and church newsletters. Target 10 paying families and track escalations as your proof.

title: Humanoid Rentals for Events and Retail
one_liner: The first profitable humanoid job is spectacle: rent Unitree-class robots plus a trained show operator to brands, malls, arenas and trade shows.
customer: Experiential-marketing agencies, retail flagships, stadium and arena marketing teams, trade-show exhibitors, casinos and theme venues. Universities renting lab time come second.
problem: Everyone else pitches humanoids as factory workers, where reliability, safety and ROI are unproven. Brands want a 'robots are here' moment now but cannot buy, program and insure a $16k robot themselves.
solution: Own 6-10 units. Sell packaged experiences (greeter, product demo, dance or boxing, photo-booth persona) with an operator, choreographer, safety marshal and event insurance. Every event doubles as a demo funnel for enterprise pilot inquiries, and later as controlled data capture.
why_now: Unitree's August 2026 IPO (about $9B) and G1 pricing near $16k make fleet capex trivial, so a robot pays back in roughly 10 event-days at $1.5-2.5k a day (my estimate). Humanoid hype is at its peak and marketing budgets are chasing it. China's robot-rental-for-events market is a proof point.
revenue_model: $2-6k a day per robot with operator, $25-60k custom activations, and sponsorship fees. Add an enterprise-pilot lead-gen fee from robot vendors later.
non_obvious_insight: Entertainment tolerates a 70% success rate and teleop, because a stumble is content. The buyer pays for attention, not productivity, so humanoid economics work here years before they work on a factory floor. Note: tariffs or restrictions on Chinese robots are a risk, so keep a non-Chinese unit option.
first_30_days: Buy 2 G1s (about $32k) and build 3 scripted 10-minute acts. Cold-pitch 40 experiential agencies, minor-league teams and mall marketing managers. Book 5 paid weekend events and film content for social proof.

title: AI-Label Pre-Flight Before You Upload
one_liner: A 'spellcheck for platform AI labels' that predicts how each service will tag and treat a file before it goes live.
customer: Social video teams, agencies, MCNs, podcast networks, and labels or distributors delivering to several DSPs, all of whom use mixed tool chains.
problem: Every major platform now labels or penalizes AI content: YouTube auto-labels (May 27), TIDAL badges and demonetizes (Jul 15), Snapchat stopped recommending fully-AI Spotlight content (Jul 31), and Spotify excludes AI persona profiles from recommendations (Aug 11). Labels can be triggered by markers in any single asset, such as one generative b-roll clip or an AI retouch, and rules differ per platform. Teams cannot predict outcomes.
solution: Upload the final export or stem set. The tool reads C2PA manifests, IPTC DigitalSourceType and XMP, runs public watermark verifiers where they exist, applies per-platform rule tables, and predicts the label and monetization outcome per service. It points to the timeline segments or assets that triggered it, drafts accurate disclosure text, and logs the result. It recommends fixes such as re-rendering a clip, and never strips manifests. Ships as plugins for Premiere, Resolve and Frame.io plus an API for DAM systems.
why_now: Platform penalties for AI labeling only became real between May and Aug 2026, and the rules differ across services. Content Credentials adoption (TikTok joined in Jul 2026) means more assets carry markers.
revenue_model: $49-499/month per team, an API at $0.02 per asset, and $2-10k/month enterprise plans.
non_obvious_insight: The market has focused on creating labels and detecting AI. Once labels carry monetization consequences, the demand is for predicting them, like SEO tools for policy. Honest teams with minor assistive AI, not cheats, are the buyers, and the product keeps disclosure accurate.
first_30_days: Build a parser on the open-source c2pa-rs library plus a rule table from published policies. Test it on 200 real videos. Offer 10 agencies a free label audit of their last 20 uploads and sell the first team plans.

title: Memory Safe-Harbor: Stop Shredding Server DRAM
one_liner: A component-level sanitization policy plus a resale desk that lets neoclouds and enterprises reuse retired DRAM, CPUs and GPUs instead of shredding whole servers.
customer: Neoclouds, colocation operators, banks and healthcare IT asset managers refreshing servers, with ITADs as the channel. They pay a fixed fee and take a resale share.
problem: Data-center hardware turns over in 12-18 months and a GPU server rack can exceed $1M. DRAM is up about 400% since early 2024. Many enterprise policies still shred whole servers, destroying volatile memory that holds no persistent data. One client reportedly gained 'eight figures' just by pre-triaging refurbish versus scrap.
solution: Publish and audit a per-server-model matrix of which components persist data (SSDs, NVDIMMs, BMC and NIC flash, TPMs) and which do not (DIMMs, most compute and mechanical parts). Get it signed off by a security auditor and the client's CISO. Then run the part-out desk. Data-bearing parts are wiped or destroyed with serialized custody. Everything else is graded, tested and sold to secondary buyers.
why_now: The 2025-26 memory price spike turns shredding into a cash-burning act. AI capex has created huge, fast-cycling retiring fleets, and Sumitomo's GreenTek acquisition shows ITAD is being bought as a trading business.
revenue_model: 40-60% resale share to the client after costs, a $10-30K policy and audit fee per client, and a per-serial chain-of-custody fee.
non_obvious_insight: 'Shred everything' is a compliance habit, not a security requirement. The barrier is organizational sign-off, not technology. Whoever ships a pre-approved risk framework gets inventory that no one else can touch.
first_30_days: Write a 10-page component sanitization matrix for the 5 most common GPU and CPU server models. Have a security-audit firm review it. Pitch 10 neocloud and colo IT asset leads and 5 mid-size ITADs. Run a one-rack pilot on revenue share.

title: Proof-of-Ingestion Traps for Creators' Content
one_liner: Plant unique, statistically detectable traps in creators' work, then probe AI models to produce evidence that the content was ingested.
customer: Newsletter, blog and podcast networks, small publishers, illustrator collectives and rights-holder collectives, plus litigation funders and law firms.
problem: Creators cannot prove that a model trained on their work, and that proof is the gating evidence for licensing and claims. Published research on copyright traps and 'radioactive' data suggests unique planted sequences can statistically reveal training use. The licensing market is forming (Suno's licensed model, label suits, Spotify deals), but information is heavily asymmetric.
solution: A plug-in adds unique fictional-but-plausible facts and phrasing patterns to text posts (and validated perturbations where it works for images and audio). A monitoring service queries major model APIs monthly with probes and issues an 'ingestion report' with p-values. Reports aggregate into collective evidence packs for licensing negotiations and claims. Detection power depends on repetition and model behavior, so start with text.
why_now: AI licensing and settlements are creating demand for evidence, probing APIs are cheap, and trap research has matured enough to productize.
revenue_model: $29-99/month per creator, $2-10k/month for publishers and collectives, $25-100k per litigation-grade study, and a fee share on licensing deals.
non_obvious_insight: Whoever produces credible evidence of ingestion becomes the toll-taker between creators and labs, like a credit bureau for training data. Traps are cheap to plant, while the evidence is priced like litigation support.
first_30_days: Seed traps in three months of posts across 20 newsletters, test six popular models with retrieval off, and publish a results note. Take a sample report to two litigation-funding shops and small-publisher trade groups.

title: Pre-Confirmation Screwworm Risk Feed for Cattle Markets
one_liner: A county-level early-warning feed that fuses news, vet reports, weather and zone announcements to give cattle buyers, auction barns and insurers days or weeks of lead time over official lab confirmation.
customer: Auction markets and sale barns, feedlots and stocker buyers, livestock lenders and insurers, and cattle-futures or ag-commodity desks. Ranchers and vet clinics are a low-price tier.
problem: New World screwworm has reached Texas and New Mexico. The UC San Diego team building a tracker says official reporting lags: 'Lab confirmation can take days or weeks.' Cattle prices, hauling rules and purchase decisions move on rumor and news before confirmation. Producers have no single source for zone status and their own exposure.
solution: A subscription feed that scores county-level risk from public and semi-public signals: state and APHIS zone announcements, extension and vet-clinic posts, local news, trap and case reports, and fly-friendly temperature and humidity. It sends SMS or email alerts and a plain-language 'movement readiness' checklist for each zone. Users can submit their own sightings, which improves the model. Sold in tiers from a $99/month producer plan to trading-desk contracts.
why_now: The screwworm reached the US Southwest in 2026, and APHIS newsroom items on 18 and 21 September 2026 show Texas releasing infested zones. The academic dashboard is a research tool, not a commercial product, and the sterile-fly response is slow to scale, so risk and compliance uncertainty will last through at least one fly season.
revenue_model: Producer and barn subscriptions at $99-500/month, insurer, lender and buyer contracts at $2-10k/month, and enterprise API fees for commodity desks.
non_obvious_insight: The academic value of the dashboard is the reporting lag itself: the UC San Diego team added media reports because 'lab confirmation can take days or weeks' (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260914102439.htm). The paying customer is anyone whose money moves on news before USDA confirms, meaning buyers, hedgers and insurers, not the county health officials the tool was built for. The lag is the product. Recent APHIS announcements show zone status is changing week to week (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/news).
first_30_days: Build a scraper and manual-curation pipeline over APHIS and Texas Animal Health Commission announcements, extension and vet feeds, and local news, plus a weather-based fly-activity index. Publish a free weekly map to gather emails. Pitch 10 sale barns and 3 commodity or insurer desks a paid pilot and sell the first 5 at a founding discount. Contact the UC San Diego team about a data and methods collaboration. Note that the APHIS screwworm page consulted in this session still said the pest was absent from the US, so confirm current case status before launch.

title: Pharmacy-Side PBM Ledger for Employers
one_liner: Independent pharmacies hold the half of the PBM ledger that employers never see, which is what the PBM actually paid the pharmacy. Pool it to run spread audits for self-insured employers, and give pharmacies a stay-or-leave calculator for their take-it-or-leave-it PBM contracts.
customer: Two sides. First, independent pharmacies, at $99-199 a month for benchmarking and a network-contract modeler. Second, self-funded local employers, school districts, counties and union funds (from 100 to 5,000 lives), plus the benefit consultants and TPAs that serve them, who pay per audit or a share of verified savings.
problem: The employer sees only what it paid the PBM. The PBM sees both sides and hides one. The pharmacy sees what it was paid and what it paid the wholesaler, but has no benchmark and no idea whether the network offer that arrives every Q4 for January 1 is worse than its peers' terms. Everyone negotiates blind. PBMs threaten a pharmacy with losing about a quarter of its business if it declines, and a plan sponsor cannot verify 'pass-through' claims.
solution: Read-only ingestion of the pharmacy's 835 remittance files and invoice costs from its pharmacy management system (PMS). Output 1) per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement benchmarked against NADAC and an anonymized peer pool. 2) A stay-or-leave model of each 2027 network offer built from the pharmacy's own claims mix. 3) With sponsor consent, a claim-level tie-out of the pharmacy-paid amounts against the employer's PBM claims file. That yields a true spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member, delivered as an audit the employer can use to renegotiate or move to a transparent PBM.
why_now: The contract season for January 2027 is happening right now, which gives a hard deadline and a free entry wedge. Employer fiduciaries are under pressure from ERISA suits over PBM costs, state PBM transparency laws and FTC scrutiny. Pharmacy closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores) have given local officials political will. OCR and LLM parsing of messy remit PDFs now makes onboarding a one-day job rather than a consulting project.
revenue_model: Pharmacy subscription of $99-199 a month, or free in exchange for data. Employer audit fees of about $8k-25k per mid-size sponsor, or 10-20% of first-year verified savings. Data licenses to state employee plans, attorneys general, employer coalitions and consultants at a higher tier.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone in the PBM fight holds half a ledger, and only the pharmacy can prove the gap. Thirty pharmacies in one county reconstruct the local school district's and county government's spread at claim level. Independents will hand this data over willingly because it is the first ammunition they have ever had against take-it-or-leave-it contracts.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 pharmacies through the state independent pharmacy association with the pitch 'we will model your 2027 PBM offers free'. Build parsers for the three biggest PBMs' remit formats (the 835 EDI standard helps). Deliver the first stay-or-leave reports. Hire a healthcare attorney to structure data-use terms, since provider-manual confidentiality clauses and HIPAA de-identification are the main risk. Offer one local school district or county a free pilot spread audit and turn the result into a one-page case study.

title: Reproduction-Gated Vulnerability Inbox for Maintainers
one_liner: A hosted security-report intake that only forwards a report if its proof-of-concept actually reproduces against the maintainer's tagged release in a sandbox, so AI-generated slop dies before a human reads it.
customer: Maintainers and foundations of widely depended-on open-source projects (paid by corporate sponsors and dependents), plus small vendors that must run a coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy under the CRA. They pay $99-499/month per project, or $2k/month sponsor-funded shields for critical projects.
problem: curl ended its bug bounty at the end of January 2026 to 'remove the incentive for people to submit crap and non-well researched reports... AI generated or not'; in the week before, 7 submissions contained no real vulnerabilities but still burned security-team time. Maintainers are also drowning in PRs, with Ladybird banning non-maintainer PRs and Rust's Clippy gamifying review, while companies float donating AI credits to maintainers instead.
solution: An intake form and GitHub App that requires a machine-checkable reproducer (Dockerfile/script/HTTP request plus the expected oracle, such as an ASAN crash, unexpected file read or assertion). The service builds the project at the reported tag in a microVM, runs the reproducer and only escalates reports that trip the oracle. Failures get instant automated feedback. Passing reports arrive at the maintainer as a verified repro bundle, deduplicated against past reports, with a suggested severity and a drafted advisory and CVE request. Logic bugs without automatic oracles go through a refundable deposit lane. Start with memory-safety classes (C/C++/Rust/Go) where oracles are objective.
why_now: January 2026 made the AI-slop-versus-security-report problem concrete and public. CRA reporting duties began in September 2026, increasing report volume and the need for a documented intake. Cheap microVM sandboxes (Firecracker-class) make per-report verification cost cents.
revenue_model: Sponsor-paid subscriptions: $99-499/month per project, funded by the top dependents (companies that already say they want to help maintainers, per the AI-credits thread). $1-2k/month for critical projects. Per-verified-report fee for small vendors with public VDPs.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone argues about banning submissions or paying for them; nobody has moved the burden of proof onto machines, and the same LLMs that write slop cannot fake a crashing sanitizer trace on the maintainer's own build. The buyer is not the burned-out maintainer with no budget but the dependents who need that maintainer to keep going. Evidence: curl closing its bounty https://www.theregister.com/2026/01/21/curl_ends_bug_bounty/; maintainers asking how to handle PR slop and pointing to tools https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47492078; Ladybird and Clippy approaches plus a call for third-party solutions https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48949019; companies wanting to donate but debating the wrong instrument (credits vs money) https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48346013.
first_30_days: Build the GitHub App and intake page for C, Rust and Go projects using sanitizer/crash oracles. Recruit 3 mid-size maintainers by replying in the PR-slop and AI-contribution Ask HN threads; run their real inbox through it in shadow mode for two weeks and report the percentage of reports filtered. Take that data to each project's top corporate dependents and ask for a $250/month sponsorship that funds the shield.

title: Valet Keys for Delegated Browser Sessions
one_liner: An enforcement layer that lets an agent act inside your logged-in bank, airline or supplier portal, but only within per-site limits such as read-only here and a spend cap there.
customer: Enterprise finance-ops, revenue-cycle and logistics teams running browser agents on portals with no API (20-500 seats), followed by builders of prosumer browser agents who need a safety story.
problem: Insiders are building agent identity (OAuth for agents), but most delegated work rides on cookies in sites with no API. The agent inherits the user's full session. Browsers offer no primitive for a user to see, scope or withdraw an agent's access. If the user is legally the one who accessed the site, as the Ninth Circuit reasoned, the user owns everything the agent does with that session.
solution: A browser extension plus enforcement proxy with per-site policy packs that classify actions (view, draft, submit, pay, change credentials) using URL, DOM and network patterns. Irreversible actions are denied by default, with spend and count caps, step-up approval and signed action receipts. Ship maintained packs for the top 200 enterprise portals (payer, carrier, marketplace seller-center and bank portals) and update them as sites change.
why_now: Browser agents went mainstream in 2026, and about 21,600 OpenClaw instances were found exposed. Machine identities outnumber humans roughly 109 to 1, and the agent-equals-user doctrine puts liability on the delegating user.
revenue_model: $15-40 per seat per month for enterprises, policy-pack subscriptions, and a per-session API price for agent vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The missing primitive is a valet key (parks the car, cannot open the trunk) for sessions. The moat is the maintained per-site action taxonomy, which is tedious, unglamorous and hard to copy.
first_30_days: Find one revenue-cycle or logistics ops team already using browser agents and build read-only plus draft-only policy packs for the 5 portals they use. Run a $2k/month pilot and log blocked actions as proof of value.

title: Customs-Verified Collateral for Inventory Lenders
one_liner: An API and reporting layer that verifies borrowers' in-transit inventory against ISF, entry, release and liquidation records, so lenders stop financing containers that do not exist.
customer: Inventory-finance and revenue-based lenders for e-commerce brands, factoring companies, ABL desks at small banks, and buyers of tariff-refund receivables. They pay per verification and per monitored loan.
problem: Lenders finance purchase orders and goods on the water. Their collateral evidence is invoices, a bill of lading PDF and the borrower's word. Fraud, double-pledging, inflated quantities and phantom shipments are a chronic loss driver in small-business trade finance. Tariffs made it worse: duties now consume a big share of landed cost, so lenders need to know what was actually declared, at what value, and whether it cleared or is held. The truth exists in CBP data that brokers see within hours. Lenders see it, if at all, weeks late through the borrower.
solution: Connect to the collateral through consent-based data paths: importer-scheduled ACE reports forwarded to a dedicated inbox, and ABI/status feeds from cooperating brokers that get paid for sharing. Reconcile each financed PO against ISF filing, entry summary, release or hold status, declared value and HTS, and (after the IEEPA ruling) refund eligibility. Deliver a loan-level 'entry-verified' status and exception alerts, such as a container that never had an ISF, a value mismatch, or an exam hold that makes collateral illiquid. The same engine verifies IEEPA refund claims for lenders advancing against them.
why_now: Inventory financing and tariff-duty financing for e-commerce brands surged in 2024-26, and lenders are absorbing losses they do not yet understand. Refund-backed lending is new since the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling and CAPE, and it needs entry-level verification. ACE reports are self-serve, so no permission from CBP is needed. Brokers are looking for revenue beyond thin filing fees.
revenue_model: $15-40 per shipment verification, or a monitoring SaaS fee of about 5-15 basis points on funded volume, with platform minimums of $2-5k a month. Brokers get a revenue share on data feeds. Add-on: refund-claim diligence packages.
non_obvious_insight: A PO and a bill of lading are easy to forge. An ISF filed before vessel loading, tied to a bond, followed by a release message from CBP, is not. It is the closest thing to a government-attested proof that goods exist and are moving. Because the importer owns the ACE data, no data-broker licensing fight is needed. Trade-finance software vendors model documents. Nobody models the entry record.
first_30_days: Approach five small inventory lenders, factors and refund-claim buyers with a manual pilot: they send 10 borrowers' entry data, and you return verified and unverified lists within 48 hours. Recruit two friendly customs brokers for feed access on consenting clients. Build the reconciliation on spreadsheets and scripts first, and charge $500-$1,500 per pilot batch. The first paid lender contract is usually a covenant addition: 'borrower must forward ACE reports monthly'.

title: Pre-Loss Home Reconstruction Dossiers for Insurance Claims
one_liner: Rebuild, in the exact quality and condition language insurers can't wave away, what a destroyed home actually had, using old appraisals, listing photos, permits and imagery.
customer: Public adjusters and policyholder-side insurance attorneys handling total-loss wildfire, hurricane and tornado claims pay $900-2,500 per dossier. Direct-to-homeowner is $495 for a basic version. Independent insurance agents later buy a 'pre-loss baseline' for their high-value clients.
problem: After a total loss, the insurer's estimate assumes builder-grade finishes and smaller square footage. The survivor's photos and receipts burned, so 'like kind and quality' becomes a memory-versus-spreadsheet fight worth tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars per house. Public adjusters reconstruct from Zillow photos and homeowner recollection, which adjusters on the other side discount.
solution: A retrospective, signed 'as-was' dossier delivered in about 5 business days. Sources: (1) any prior purchase or refinance appraisal the homeowner has (borrowers are entitled to copies) or can get through the lender or servicer; (2) archived MLS photos and remarks from the last sale; (3) permit and remodel history; (4) assessor quality and size records; (5) historical aerial and street-level imagery. A licensed appraiser assigns the standard Q1-Q6 quality and C1-C6 condition ratings, lists the finishes and features, and estimates replacement cost at that quality level.
why_now: The January 2025 Los Angeles fires destroyed roughly 16,000 structures, and many claims are still being contested in late 2026. Every wildfire and hurricane season adds more total losses. Insurers are tightening costs and leaning on adjuster software. Photo and record archives from prior sales are now digital and searchable, so the reconstruction is a 5-day job.
revenue_model: Flat fee per dossier only. USPAP forbids contingent appraisal fees, and independence is the product's credibility. Volume pricing for public adjuster firms. $99/yr 'baseline vault' (current LiDAR, photos and Q/C ratings) sold through independent insurance agents in wildfire and hurricane zones, who carry E&O exposure when clients are underinsured.
non_obvious_insight: The best pre-loss evidence in America already exists, sitting in lender closing files, appraisal workfiles kept five years and old MLS pages. Nobody connects it to claims. A neutral licensed appraiser's dated interior photos and Q/C ratings carry far more weight with an insurer than a homeowner's testimony. Those disputes are won at the finish level (cabinetry, flooring, millwork), not on square footage, and the appraiser's rating vocabulary is what claims examiners recognize.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 appraisers in Los Angeles County who lost work. Build one dossier template. Offer 5 free pilot dossiers to 2-3 public adjuster firms and one policyholder attorney working Altadena or Pacific Palisades cases, and measure how much the insurer's revised offer moves. Then charge $1,500 per dossier and use the measured lift as the sales pitch.

title: Distressed Recycling Equipment Exchange
one_liner: A broker-refurbisher that moves equipment from failed US recycling plants to funded buyers abroad, with commissioning included.
customer: Recyclers in India, Mexico, Turkey, Southeast Asia and Africa building capacity (buyers), sourcing from receivers, lenders and former owners.
problem: More than a quarter of US PET recycling capacity closed in 12 months (7 of about 30). Ascend Elements filed Chapter 11 in April 2026, Li-Cycle went bankrupt in 2025, and Solarcycle paused a plant. Washing lines, extruders, optical sorters and reactors are stranded, while India earmarked about $166M to subsidize recycling capacity.
solution: Catalog equipment with photos and condition reports, bundle it into 'line packages', refurbish and test, ship, and send a commissioning team. Give buyers financing-ready documentation and give receivers a fast, credible exit.
why_now: 2025-26 produced an unusual wave of high-spec recycling plant failures, and subsidy money abroad creates buyers, both at once.
revenue_model: 10-20% commission on sales plus refurbishment and commissioning fees.
non_obvious_insight: General industrial liquidators do not know which line is a working PET wash line. Domain knowledge plus buyer matching is the margin, and it grows every time another recycler fails.
first_30_days: Contact the receivers and lenders for the 7 closed reclaimers and other failed plants. Build an equipment inventory with photos. Pre-sell to 5 Indian or Mexican buyers before taking on any inventory.

title: Charged Battery Cylinders for Market Traders
one_liner: Deliver and swap standardised 2 kWh LFP packs daily to market traders, the way gas cylinders are sold.
customer: Market traders, salons, food vendors and phone-charging kiosks in Lagos, Kano, Nairobi and Accra.
problem: These businesses run petrol and diesel generators or lose sales in outages, and cannot afford upfront batteries even as Africa imports more battery dollars than panels.
solution: Rugged handled LFP packs, solar-charged at rooftop depots and swapped daily by motorcycle couriers on a per-swap subscription. The wedge is 200 vendors around one market served from a depot with about 60 packs.
why_now: LFP cell prices are low, the fuel-price shock hurts generator users, and distributed solar is already scaling faster than utility supply.
revenue_model: $0.80-1.50 per swap, with 30-40% gross margin at about 70% pack utilisation.
non_obvious_insight: Small traders buy energy the way they buy gas, in small frequent delivered units. A swap network amortises battery cost across many users and removes the upfront barrier.
first_30_days: Build 30 packs and run swaps for 20 vendors at one market to measure utilisation and pack cycle life.

title: Refundable-Deposit Demand Proof for Indie Hardware
one_liner: A hosted reservation page that lets small hardware creators collect refundable $20-$50 deposits at tiered locked prices, giving them price-elasticity data and a demand certificate before they commit to a campaign or a factory MOQ.
customer: First- and second-time hardware and game creators planning a Kickstarter or Indiegogo launch, plus the small factories and pledge-manager agencies that advise them. Payer is the creator.
problem: Kickstarter median funding is $7,060 versus a $64,567 average, and Indiegogo's top performers all 'arrived with an audience already built.' Small creators have followers but no proof anyone will pay, so they either launch blind or over-order inventory.
solution: A Stripe Connect-based landing page where each deposit charges the creator's own account (no funds held by us) and is refunded on request. Visitors choose among three locked-in price tiers (A/B-testing price), and a referral queue rewards sharing. The dashboard shows deposit count by country, price-tier elasticity and expected launch-day conversion. A 'demand certificate' PDF can be handed to factories negotiating MOQ or to lenders offering inventory financing. Deposits convert with one click to day-one pledges on launch.
why_now: Big brands proved the pattern in 2025-26. eufyMake ran a $50 deposit to lock a $1,499 price before its April 2025 Kickstarter and raised over $10M in 14 hours. Creality's refundable $50 deposit unlocked a $649 VIP price for its filament maker, and the goal was hit in about 16.5 minutes. Meanwhile Indiegogo retired Flexible Funding in October 2025, so both platforms are all-or-nothing and the cost of launching without proof is higher.
revenue_model: $299 setup plus 1.5% of deposits processed, a $999 launch-readiness package (demand certificate, pricing test, launch-day email sequence), and $49/mo for post-launch late-pledge and pre-order pages.
non_obvious_insight: The most successful launches of 2025-26 did not start on Kickstarter. They started with money-backed waitlists. eufyMake opened a $50 deposit pre-order scheme to lock a $1,499 price ahead of the April 29 Kickstarter (https://www.notebookcheck.net/Anker-EufyMake-E1-UV-printer-Pre-order-deposit-scheme-now-open.999622.0.html) and then raised $46.76M from 17,822 backers (https://www.entrepreneur.com/business-news/3d-printer-breaks-kickstarter-record-raises-44m/493857). Creality took $50 refundable deposits for VIP $649 pricing on the M1 (https://makers101.com/creality-filament-maker-m1-shredder-r1-live-tracker/). Kickstarter's own pre-launch page only collects follows, and the ecosystem is top-heavy (median $7,060 vs average $64,567, and 'all Indiegogo top performers arrived with an audience', https://www.tcf.team/blog/q1-2026-crowdfunding-report). A deposit is a far stronger demand signal than a follower, and small creators have no tool to run one, no way to test three price points, and no artefact factories will trust.
first_30_days: Build the landing page and Stripe Connect flow in 2 weeks. Pitch 10 creators with live 'coming soon' pages on Kickstarter, offering a free pilot in exchange for a case study. Run a $20-$50 deposit test with one creator (target 150+ deposits) and document the elasticity result. Publish the case study on r/Kickstarter, BackerKit-focused groups and crowdfunding Discords, then charge the next 5 creators.

title: Parametric Recovery Cover for Tourism Towns
one_liner: Annual parametric policies bought by destination tourism boards that pay out within days when fire, smoke, flood or road closures crater visitor demand, even with no physical damage.
customer: Destination marketing organizations and county or city tourism authorities in single-access, hazard-exposed resort towns (Estes Park, Truckee/Tahoe, Big Bear, Gatlinburg, Outer Banks, Asheville, Maui), funded by lodging taxes (transient occupancy tax, TOT) with $50-500K premium budgets.
problem: Business-interruption cover requires physical damage, and civil-authority riders are short. After Lahaina, Asheville and Caldor, the losses came from closed roads, smoke and perception, not damaged hotels. TOT revenue funds recovery marketing and services, and it collapses exactly when the town most needs to advertise. Retail insurers are retreating from these towns and small lodging and restaurants cannot buy adequate cover.
solution: We design tourism-specific indices and place the cover. Triggers use hazard evidence (evacuation orders, AQI days over threshold, DOT road-closure days) confirmed by an occupancy drop versus baseline (STR/hotel data such as AirDNA). Payout scales are calibrated to historical TOT dips. The policyholder is the DMO, which re-grants through its existing marketing and small-business grant programs. Capacity comes from a fronting carrier or parametric MGA plus reinsurers and ILS. We deliver index design, backtests, placement and the claims data oracle.
why_now: Reinsurance is softening fast: Howden reports property-cat risk-adjusted rates down up to 25% at 1 June 2026 after -16% and -14.7% earlier, with record capital (about $790B, secondary source). Niche capacity is now cheap while retail carriers still retreat. Cat bond issuance hit records in H1 2026 (about $18B). Travel booking windows are about 33 days, so a fast cash-funded comeback campaign can restore bookings quickly.
revenue_model: Broker/MGA-style commission of 12-18% of premium, plus index licensing and annual re-modeling fees. Ten towns at about $150K average premium and 15% commission is roughly $225K in year one, scaling through state travel associations.
non_obvious_insight: Tourism loss after disasters is mostly access and perception, not damage. A public tourism board is the rare buyer that can purchase parametric cover and redistribute it to small businesses that could never qualify individually. The lodging-tax series is a clean, public, monthly loss history no adjuster touched. Public-entity buyers also sidestep the homeowner rate-filing regime that strangles retail products.
first_30_days: Backtest four past events (East Troublesome/Estes Park 2020, Caldor/Tahoe 2021, Lahaina 2023, Helene/Asheville 2024) using public TOT reports, AQI and road-closure logs. Produce 'what you would have received' one-pagers. Pitch 10 DMO executive directors and 3 state travel associations. Get a parametric MGA or fronting partner to quote. Target the first bound policy in the spring 2027 budget and fire-season renewal window.

title: Scam Recovery Desk for Community Banks
one_liner: Banks buy scam detection, but the untapped money is recovery: stablecoin issuers, receiving banks and exchanges can freeze funds if someone asks fast and correctly.
customer: Community banks and credit unions ($500M-$10B assets) that increasingly eat scam reimbursements. American Banker (2026-07-22) puts bank-side scam losses at $68B, against the FTC's $15.9B of consumer-reported losses.
problem: A community bank's fraud analyst has hours before funds move on. They don't know who to call at receiving banks, exchanges or issuer compliance desks. They have no standard evidence pack, so recoveries run to a few percent and losses are written off as a cost of doing business.
solution: A 24/7 recovery desk plus software. When a victim reports a scam, the desk traces the funds (wire, Zelle and ACH recall, plus on-chain tracing for crypto off-ramps). It sends recall, 314(b) and law-enforcement freeze requests with pre-validated evidence packs to a maintained directory of receiving-institution and issuer contacts, then tracks outcomes. The desk is paid a share of every dollar recovered.
why_now: FTC losses hit a record $15.9B in 2025, and scam flows increasingly touch stablecoins. The Senate Democrats' Tether report (2026-09-28) raises pressure on issuers to respond quickly, and GENIUS-era issuers must be able to honor lawful freeze orders (verify exact text).
revenue_model: 15-25% contingency on recovered funds plus a flat monthly retainer for 24/7 coverage.
non_obvious_insight: Recovery rates depend on speed and relationships, not analytics, so a maintained contact directory and playbook is an operations moat. Stablecoins are counterintuitively the most freezable scam rail, more so than wires or Zelle, if you know the freeze path.
first_30_days: Offer five community banks a free post-mortem of their last 90 days of scam cases and estimate the recoverable share. Hire two ex-bank fraud investigators. Sign two contingency pilots and build the first version of the issuer and receiving-bank contact directory.

title: Agent-Bookable Gateway for Local Trades
one_liner: A per-business endpoint that lets consumers' AI agents get a photo-based quote, hold a slot and pay a deposit at a local trade without a phone call.
customer: House cleaners, junk-removal crews, pressure washers, mobile detailers, movers, handymen and groomers (1-15 staff) with weak or template websites.
problem: Consumers increasingly ask assistants to 'find and book' local help. Agents can't get a price, slot or deposit from a local trade without a call, so trades are invisible to agent-driven demand. Reviews and SEO matter less than being machine-readable and bookable.
solution: Each business gets an agent endpoint: photo-to-quote with vision models, service area and rules (minimum job, blackout dates), live slot holds, and a payment link for the deposit. It is exposed through structured data, an OpenAPI or MCP interface, and registered with agent platforms and directories. Owners set guardrails and approve borderline quotes by text.
why_now: Consumer agents and agentic-commerce protocols emerged in 2025-26 (prior knowledge), vision models can price photo-priceable jobs, and 46% of small firms already use AI, so owners are open to the concept.
revenue_model: $49/month plus a 3-5% booking fee on agent-originated jobs.
non_obvious_insight: The next website is a callable endpoint, and the first vertical where agents can close is the one where jobs are priceable from photos. Scheduling incumbents hold the data but may not expose a public agent interface, so a neutral gateway can win a directory position.
first_30_days: Sign 20 operators in two photo-priceable verticals, publish their endpoints and test with the major assistants' agent modes plus manual concierge. Measure agent-originated bookings and quote accuracy.

title: Rent Seasonal Nitrate Treatment, Don't Build Plants
one_liner: Trailer-mounted nitrate-removal skids rented to small farm-belt utilities only for the 60-120 days a year when river or shallow-well nitrate spikes.
customer: Small and mid-size utilities (500-10,000 people) in Iowa, Nebraska, Illinois, Minnesota, Kansas and Wisconsin that draw from rivers or shallow aquifers. Systems with recent nitrate MCL violations are first. The utility pays, and state programs may help.
problem: More than 60M Americans are served from elevated-nitrate sources, and the 10 ppm limit dates from 1991. EPA's cancer review has stalled since 2023, and its research office is gone. Small rural systems bear treatment costs alone. A permanent $2-10M plant is out of reach for them, though the exceedance is seasonal.
solution: A fleet of containerized nitrate-selective ion-exchange skids sized 0.25-2 MGD. Include resin regeneration, brine logistics (the make-or-break piece, so pre-agree the disposal route with the wastewater plant or a hauler), operator training and remote monitoring. Priced as a seasonal service, per 1,000 gallons treated with a seasonal minimum. Start asset-light by leasing skids from an existing ion-exchange OEM.
why_now: Federal action on nitrate is stalled, so relief is not coming from Washington. Broad drought followed by heavy runoff swings nitrate hard. The FY2026 $7.2B SRF pool makes states receptive to flexible compliance solutions. The 10 ppm limit is still enforceable today.
revenue_model: Seasonal rental of $15-40k/month per skid plus per-gallon regeneration and brine fees, under 3-5 year master service agreements.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume compliance means permanent capital. But nitrate is a peak problem (Des Moines Water Works runs its removal plant only during high-nitrate stretches, from my background knowledge), so the winning model sells the peak, not the plant. A rental converts an unfundable capital project into a fundable operating line.
first_30_days: Pull three years of nitrate MCL violations from the public SDWIS database and build a list of 100 systems. Call five directly and through a state rural water association. Sign an MOU with one ion-exchange OEM for lease-back skids, and get one utility to agree to a paid pilot for spring 2027.
